albumBackground:
Karl Richter's 1961 recording of Johann Sebastian Bach's Mass in B minor (BWV 232) with the Münchener Bach-Chor and Münchener Bach-Orchester remains one of the monumental achievements in 20th-century classical discography. Recorded at the Musikhochschule München and released on Archiv Produktion / Deutsche Grammophon in 1962, this performance established the mid-century gold standard for Bach interpretation. Richter brought a rare balance of architectural discipline, dramatic intensity, and spiritual reverence to Bach's final sacred masterpiece, supported by an extraordinary vocal line-up that included soprano Maria Stader, contralto Hertha Töpper, tenor Ernst Haefliger, and bass Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau.

Technically, the recording session was a triumph of early stereo analogue engineering. Produced by Karl-Heinz Schneider and engineered by sound balance master Walther Alfred Wettler, the production utilized valve-driven Neumann microphone setups, custom German mixing consoles, and high-quality 2-track master tape machines. The acoustic space of the Munich hall was captured with remarkable spaciousness, allowing the complex contrapuntal lines of the choir to remain distinct even during full orchestral climaxes. Richter's deliberate tempi and emphasis on instrumental clarity—highlighted by Adolf Scherbaum's virtuosic high-trumpet playing—offered an expressive alternative to the later historically informed performance (HIP) movement.

This specific Japanese LP issue, titled 'Bach: Messe in h-moll (Chöre und Arien)' (Catalog No. MGX7096, released by Polydor K.K. under Deutsche Grammophon in 1978), compiles essential choruses and arias onto a single LP format. Japanese DG pressings from the late 1970s are revered among audiophile collectors for their ultra-quiet virgin vinyl formulations, flat frequency response, precise spindle centering, and meticulous jacket craftsmanship. Complete with Japanese insert notes and the iconic DG obi strip, this pressing delivers an exceptionally pristine listening window into Richter's timeless Bach legacy.

tracklist.title: Kyrie eleison (I) (Chorus)
tracklist.whatToListenFor: Listen for the monumental opening choral entrance rising above the organ and string continuo. The Japanese LP pressing renders the hall acoustics with immense depth, preserving vocal separation across the soundstage without inner-groove congestion.

tracklist.title: Cum Sancto Spiritu (Chorus)
tracklist.whatToListenFor: Pay close attention to Adolf Scherbaum's high-register trumpet work soaring over the rapid fugal choral lines. The vinyl master retains brilliant treble sheen without harsh sibilance or tracking distortion.

tracklist.title: Credo in unum Deum / Patrem omnipotentem (Chorus)
Crucifixus (Chorus)
tracklist.whatToListenFor: Listen to the steady descending chromatic passacaglia bassline and the whispered vocal entries. The ultra-quiet Japanese vinyl surface lets the low-level acoustic decay and room ambience shine through.

tracklist.title: Sanctus (Chorus)
tracklist.whatToListenFor: Focus on the six-part choral counterpoint and swinging triple meter anchored by crisp timpani and brass fanfares. The dynamic swing from delicate vocal phrases to full orchestral tutti is exceptionally wide.

tracklist.title: Agnus Dei (Aria - Contralto)
tracklist.whatToListenFor: Hertha Töpper's mournful contralto timbre is accompanied by unison violins. Notice the intimate mid-range warmth and natural string bow textures brought out by early 1960s tube electronics.

vinylTip: For optimal playback of this Japanese Polydor K.K. pressing (MGX7096), align your cartridge with an advanced line-contact or MicroRidge stylus to smoothly track the dense choral passages near the center label. Set tracking force to around 1.6–1.8 grams to maintain bass authority and avoid mistracking on high-register brass crests.
recommendedMood: Quiet Sunday morning with a freshly brewed pour-over coffee, immersed in sacred Baroque grandeur and analogue tube warmth.
